## FAQs about IT consulting and vCIO services
Q: What is a vCIO?
A: A vCIO, or virtual CIO, is a part-time, outsourced chief information officer. You get the strategic side of IT leadership (a technology roadmap, budget planning, risk and compliance oversight, and vendor decisions) without the cost of a full-time executive. For a small business, it is the difference between making technology decisions reactively and making them on a plan.
Q: What does a vCIO do for a small business?
A: A vCIO sets the technology roadmap, budget, and risk priorities for a small business: deciding what to invest in next, how to budget for it, which risks to close first, and when a system should be replaced, consolidated, or moved to the cloud. Ghosxt delivers this directly through owner Ulises Paiz, an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience, at published pricing rather than as a full-time hire.
Q: How is IT consulting different from your managed IT service?
A: Managed IT keeps the systems running day to day: monitoring, patching, help desk, backup. IT consulting and the vCIO role sit above that and answer the strategic questions: what to invest in next year, how to budget for it, which risks to close first, whether a system should move to the cloud, and how to meet a compliance requirement. Managed clients get quarterly vCIO planning included; consulting is also available as a standalone engagement.
Q: Can I hire you for consulting without switching IT providers?
A: Yes. We offer standalone IT consulting and project work (a security assessment, a cloud-migration plan, a compliance roadmap, or vendor and contract review) without requiring you to move your day-to-day IT to us. We will give you an honest, vendor-neutral read on where you stand and what to do next.
Q: Do you help with compliance like HIPAA, CMMC, or SOC 2?
A: Yes. As an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience, compliance strategy is core to the consulting work: HIPAA for medical practices, NIST 800-171 and CMMC for defense contractors, SOC 2 readiness for SaaS and technology companies, and PCI for businesses that take cards. We translate the framework into a prioritized plan and the documentation an assessor expects.
Q: What size business needs a vCIO?
A: Typically businesses from about 10 to 100 employees that depend on technology but are too small to justify a full-time IT director or CIO. If technology decisions are being made by whoever is least busy, if your IT spend feels random, or if a compliance or growth milestone is forcing the issue, a vCIO is the right-sized answer.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

# Managed Detection & Response (MDR)

Ghosxt, run by an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience, provides managed detection and response for small businesses across Monterey County and surrounding areas: a 24/7 SOC watching endpoints, network and cloud, human-reviewed alerts and real containment when something is found, at published pricing.

Managed Detection & Response (MDR): at a glance
## Alerts are not the same as being watched
An alert nobody is watching at 2am is not protection, it's a log file. Ghosxt delivers managed detection and response with a 24/7 SOC for California small businesses: continuous monitoring across endpoints, network, and cloud, human-reviewed alerts, and real containment action, the SOC-level coverage a large enterprise runs in-house, sized and priced for a small business, from an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience.
Modern security tools generate a lot of alerts: endpoint detection, firewall logs, cloud sign-in events, email security flags. Most small businesses have some of these tools already and nobody actually watching the output in real time. An alert that sits in a dashboard until Monday morning is not protection during the 60 hours that follow it.
MDR is the human layer that makes those tools worth having: an analyst correlating signals across your endpoints, network, and cloud environment, deciding in real time what's a real threat, and taking action, not just forwarding you an email.
## Why an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience is different here
Threat detection and response is the exact discipline Ghosxt's founder practiced inside DoD networks, where an unwatched alert was never an acceptable outcome. That standard is what we apply to a small business environment: real analysis and containment, not a managed tool subscription with no one actually behind it.

## Where this fits with what we already do
## Managed Detection & Response FAQs
Q: What's the difference between MDR and the EDR we already have?
A: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) is the sensor sitting on each device generating alerts. MDR is the 24/7 human service that watches those alerts (and the ones from your network and cloud environment), correlates them, decides what's actually a threat, and acts on it. EDR without MDR behind it is a stream of alerts nobody is reliably watching at 2am.
Q: Isn't this the same as a SOC?
A: MDR is how a small business gets SOC-level coverage without building one. A traditional Security Operations Center is a room full of analysts, realistic for a large enterprise, not a 20-person business. MDR delivers the same 24/7 monitoring and response as a service, sized and priced for a small business instead.
Q: Will this replace our IT provider?
A: No, it works alongside your managed IT. MDR is the security-monitoring layer; managed IT is the day-to-day operational layer. When we deliver both, they're coordinated under one roof instead of two vendors pointing fingers during an incident.
Q: What happens when a real threat is detected?
A: A human analyst reviews the alert, confirms whether it's a genuine threat, and takes containment action directly (isolating a device, disabling a compromised account) rather than just emailing you a notification and waiting for a callback. You're informed as it happens, not after the fact.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## https://ghosxt.com/penetration-testing

Title: Penetration Testing for Small Business | Ghosxt
Meta description: We scope and coordinate manual, adversarial penetration testing for small business networks and web apps, overseen by an engineer with DoD infrastructure.

# Penetration Testing for Small Business
A vulnerability scanner tells you what's theoretically wrong. A penetration test tells you what an attacker could actually do with it. Ghosxt scopes and coordinates manual, adversarial testing on Central Coast small business networks and web applications, overseen by an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience, not a scanner running on autopilot.
Scoped and coordinated by an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience: manual testing, not an automated scan with a report slapped on it.
Penetration Testing: at a glance
## Scanning finds what's known. Testing finds what's exploitable.
Automated vulnerability scanning (the kind we run continuously as part of managed cybersecurity) checks your systems against a database of known weaknesses and flags what it finds. It is fast, cheap, and necessary. It is not the same thing as penetration testing.
A penetration test is a person, actively trying to get in: chaining a misconfigured share here to a reused password there to an unpatched service somewhere else, the same way a real attacker strings together small weaknesses into a real breach. A scan tells you a door might be unlocked. A test tells you whether someone can actually walk through it, and what they'd find on the other side.
## Why an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience is different here
Most penetration tests sold to small businesses are a scan with a formatted report and a consultant's summary on top. Ghosxt is run by an engineer with prior DoD and federal contractor infrastructure experience, someone who has tested and defended real networks, not just read about how attackers operate.
That means testing that reflects how your business actually gets attacked, not a generic checklist, and a report that tells you plainly what's exploitable, what's theoretical, and what to fix first.

### External Network Testing
### Internal Network Testing
### Web Application Testing
### Wireless & Physical Assessment
### Social Engineering & Phishing
### Report, Remediation & Retest
## Find out what a real attacker could actually reach
## Where this fits with what we already do
## Penetration Testing FAQs
Q: How is penetration testing different from vulnerability scanning?
A: Vulnerability scanning is automated and continuous: a tool checks your systems against a database of known weaknesses on a schedule. Penetration testing is manual and adversarial: a real engineer actively tries to break in, chain small weaknesses together, and see how far they can get, the same way an actual attacker would. Most cyber-insurance carriers and compliance frameworks treat them as complementary, not interchangeable: continuous scanning catches known issues fast, and periodic testing catches the exploitable paths a scanner can't see.
Q: How often should we test?
A: Annually is the common baseline, and after any major change: a new application, a network redesign, a merger, or an acquisition. Some cyber-insurance policies and compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, CMMC) specify their own minimum cadence, which we'll confirm applies to you during scoping.
Q: Do we need this for cyber insurance or compliance?
A: Often, yes. Many cyber-insurance renewals now ask whether you've had a penetration test in the last 12 months, and PCI DSS explicitly requires one annually and after significant changes. We'll tell you plainly whether your policy or framework requires it, and provide the documentation carriers and assessors expect.
Q: Will testing disrupt our systems?
A: We scope testing windows and methods around your operations: production-safe techniques, agreed timing, and a clear rules-of-engagement document signed before anything starts. Disruptive techniques (like actual exploitation of a fragile system) are called out and approved in advance, not sprung on you.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?

Zero Trust Security: at a glance
## Zero Trust is an architecture, not a product
"Trusted because it's inside the network" is exactly how a stolen laptop or a phished password turns into a full breach. Zero Trust flips that: nothing is trusted by default: every user, device, and connection has to prove itself, every time. Ghosxt builds Zero Trust architecture for Central Coast small businesses using the tools you likely already own, configured to actually enforce it.
No single tool gets you to Zero Trust, and nobody selling one box that does is telling you the whole story. Zero Trust is a set of principles applied consistently across identity, devices, and network: verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume a breach has already happened somewhere so you limit what it can reach.
For most small businesses, the building blocks already exist inside Microsoft 365 and your existing firewall (Conditional Access, device compliance policies, network segmentation), just rarely configured to actually enforce any of it. That's the gap we close.
## Why an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience is different here
Zero Trust originated in the environments Ghosxt's founder worked inside directly: DoD networks where "trusted because it's internal" was never an acceptable assumption. That's federal-grade discipline applied to a small business budget, not a marketing term borrowed from an enterprise vendor's slide deck.

## Zero Trust FAQs
Q: What is Zero Trust in plain terms?
A: Zero Trust means no user, device, or connection is trusted by default just because it's inside your network. Every request has to prove who it is, that the device is healthy, and that it only gets access to what it actually needs, every time, not just at login. It's an architecture and a set of practices, not a single product you buy.
Q: Do we need new hardware to do this?
A: Usually not. Most of Zero Trust for a small business is configuration of tools you likely already have (Microsoft 365 Conditional Access, identity policies, and network segmentation on your existing firewall) rather than new hardware purchases. We'll tell you plainly if something genuinely needs replacing.
Q: How does this fit with Microsoft 365?
A: Microsoft 365 and Entra ID already include most of the building blocks (Conditional Access, phishing-resistant MFA, device compliance policies); they're just rarely configured to actually enforce Zero Trust principles out of the box. We turn on and tune what you're already paying for.
Q: Is Zero Trust only for large enterprises?
A: No. The term originated in large-enterprise security, but the core practices (enforce MFA everywhere, give people only the access they need, segment the network so one compromised device can't reach everything) are exactly as valuable, and just as achievable, for a 10-person business as a 10,000-person one.

## FAQs about network design
Q: Do you replace our existing equipment, or work with what we have?
A: Both, depending on what is in the rack. If your existing firewall and switches are still under support and capable of doing the job, we configure them properly and document them. If they are end-of-life, undersized, or insecure by design, we replace what needs replacing and reuse the rest.
Q: What firewall vendors do you deploy?
A: We evaluate on real firewall capability, licensing model, centralized management, and integrated threat feeds rather than brand loyalty. Cisco Meraki MX is one of the firewalls we deploy, depending on the environment. We are vendor-neutral and pick the right tool for the size of business, the throughput needed, and your budget. We do not deploy ISP-provided routers as firewalls.
Q: Why do small businesses need VLANs?
A: VLANs separate traffic that should never see each other: guest Wi-Fi from production, security cameras and POS terminals from office computers, IoT devices from servers. Without segmentation, a compromised printer can give an attacker direct access to your domain controller. With segmentation, the same compromise is contained to one segment and goes nowhere.
Q: Can you handle multi-site networks?
A: Yes. Site-to-site IPsec VPN, SD-WAN, and full hub-and-spoke designs depending on the use case. Common patterns include a Salinas headquarters connected to a Watsonville cooler and a Hollister yard, with remote workers tunneling in from across the state or the country.
Q: Do we get a network diagram and documentation?
A: Yes. Every deployment ends with a written runbook, a current network diagram, IP scheme documentation, switch and firewall configuration backups, and credentials handed over to you in your password manager. You own all of it. You are not locked to us.

A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## https://ghosxt.com/ctpat

Title: C-TPAT Cybersecurity Compliance | Ghosxt

# C-TPAT Compliance Starts With Your IT Security.
CBP's updated Minimum Security Criteria require a dedicated cybersecurity program, and "our IT guy handles it" is not one. Ghosxt, run by an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience, helps importers, carriers, freight forwarders, 3PLs and customs brokers across Monterey County and surrounding areas meet and maintain the C-TPAT cybersecurity criteria, at published pricing.
C-TPAT Compliance: at a glance
## The Program That Secures U.S. Trade.
C-TPAT (Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism) is a voluntary CBP program that creates a partnership between U.S. Customs and the private sector to strengthen global supply chains against terrorism, smuggling, and now: cyber threats.
Members receive tangible trade benefits, including reduced inspections, faster processing, and trusted trader status, in exchange for meeting and maintaining CBP's Minimum Security Criteria. Cybersecurity is now a core section of those criteria.
- Fewer CBP Examinations Members experience significantly fewer physical cargo inspections, reducing delays and costs.
- Front-of-Line Processing Priority processing at ports of entry and access to FAST lanes at U.S.-Canada and U.S.-Mexico borders.
- Trusted Trader Status Mutual recognition with partner programs like AEO (EU), FAST (Canada/Mexico), and others globally.
- Competitive Advantage Partners and clients increasingly require or prefer working with C-TPAT certified companies.
## The Cybersecurity Requirements: And How We Cover Them
CBP's Minimum Security Criteria include six cybersecurity requirements. Ghosxt addresses every single one.
### Risk Assessments
CBP requires members to conduct regular IT security risk assessments to identify vulnerabilities in systems used for supply chain operations.
We conduct a full network and systems vulnerability assessment, document findings in a format aligned with CBP validation requirements, and provide a remediation roadmap.
### Access Controls
Systems must have controls limiting access to authorized users only. Multi-factor authentication, role-based access, and user account management are expected.
We implement and document MFA, Active Directory policies, privileged access management, and access reviews, then produce the evidence CBP validators look for.
### Security Awareness Training
Employees with access to IT systems and supply chain data must receive regular cybersecurity awareness training, including how to identify and report suspicious activity.
We deliver role-based training covering phishing, social engineering, password hygiene, and incident reporting, with completion records you can show CBP.
### Incident Response Plan
Members must maintain a documented incident response plan for cybersecurity breaches and provide evidence of its testing and maintenance.
We write, implement, and test your incident response plan (including tabletop exercises) and maintain it as part of ongoing managed services. Full documentation provided.
### IT Infrastructure Security
Hardware and software used in supply chain operations must be patched, documented, and protected with appropriate security controls, including endpoint protection and network segmentation.

## CMMC & NIST 800-171 FAQs
Q: Who actually needs CMMC?
A: Any business in the defense supply chain that handles federal contract information (FCI) or controlled unclassified information (CUI), whether prime contractors or, increasingly, their subcontractors. If your DoD contracts include DFARS clause 252.204-7012, CMMC is coming for you. Level 1 covers FCI; Level 2 covers CUI and maps to the 110 controls of NIST SP 800-171.
Q: What's the difference between CMMC Level 1 and Level 2?
A: Level 1 is 17 basic safeguarding practices for FCI, met with an annual self-assessment. Level 2 is the full 110 controls of NIST 800-171 for CUI, and for most contracts requires a third-party (C3PAO) assessment every three years. We determine which applies to your contracts before doing anything else, so you are not over- or under-building.
Q: We're just a subcontractor: do we still need it?
A: Very likely yes. Primes are required to flow CMMC requirements down to subcontractors who touch FCI or CUI. Many small subs are now being told by their prime that they need to show compliance to keep the work. Getting ahead of that is how you keep contracts instead of losing them to a compliant competitor.
Q: Can you get us a SPRS score and write our SSP and POA&M?
A: No. We do not write your System Security Plan (SSP) or Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M), and we do not calculate or submit your SPRS score. What we do is set up and harden the Microsoft 365 GCC High environment those documents describe, with Intune, Defender for Business, and Conditional Access, and arrange your compliance assessment through a third-party assessor.
Q: Do you set up Microsoft 365 GCC High?
A: Yes. We set up and harden Microsoft 365 GCC High for small defense contractors and subcontractors: Intune for device management, Defender for Business for threat protection, and Conditional Access for access policies, configured to what your contracts require.
Q: Who performs our CMMC assessment?
A: Not us. Ghosxt does not perform your official CMMC assessment and does not author your SSP, POA&M, or other compliance documentation. Your assessment is arranged through a third-party assessor, and we build and harden the Microsoft 365 GCC High environment that assessment evaluates.
Q: Do you perform the official CMMC assessment?
A: No. The formal Level 2 certification is performed by an accredited C3PAO, and a credible provider should not both prepare you and certify you. We set up and harden the Microsoft 365 GCC High environment being assessed; the assessment itself is arranged through a third-party assessor.
Q: How long does CMMC readiness take?
A: It depends on your starting point and scope, but a focused small-business effort is typically a few months. What Ghosxt builds and hardens is the Microsoft 365 GCC High environment scoped to your CUI, rather than securing your entire environment to the same level.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

HIPAA does not care that you run a two-provider clinic or a small specialty practice, if you store electronic patient data, the Security Rule applies in full, and a single breach can bring an investigation that asks for documentation you may not have. ## See where your practice stands on HIPAA
## The document that's almost always missing
## HIPAA IT compliance FAQs
Q: What does HIPAA actually require of our IT?
A: The HIPAA Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information (ePHI): a documented security risk analysis, access controls with unique logins and MFA, encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, audit logging, secure backup and a contingency plan, and signed Business Associate Agreements with vendors who touch ePHI. We implement and document all of it.
Q: Do small practices really get audited or fined?
A: Yes. Enforcement is overwhelmingly driven by breaches, and small practices are breached constantly: a stolen laptop, a phishing email, a misconfigured cloud share. When that happens, the Office for Civil Rights asks for your risk analysis and safeguards, and 'we are too small' is not a defense. The fines and breach-notification costs routinely dwarf the cost of doing it right.
Q: Is Microsoft 365 HIPAA compliant?
A: Microsoft 365 can be used in a HIPAA-compliant way, but it is not compliant out of the box, and a license alone does not make you compliant. You need the right plan, a signed BAA with Microsoft, and the tenant actually configured: MFA, encryption, access controls, audit logging, and email protections. We handle that configuration and the documentation that proves it.
Q: Do you sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA)?
A: Yes. As your IT provider with access to systems that store ePHI, we are a business associate, and we sign a BAA defining our responsibilities. We also make sure every other vendor in your stack that touches ePHI (cloud, backup, email) has a BAA in place, which is a gap we find in most practices.
Q: What is a Security Risk Analysis and do we need one?
A: A Security Risk Analysis (SRA) is the documented, periodic assessment of risks to your ePHI that the HIPAA Security Rule explicitly requires, and it is the single most commonly missing document when a practice is investigated. We perform it, document it, and turn the findings into a prioritized remediation plan, then keep it current.
Q: What happens if we have a breach?
A: We help you respond: contain it, determine what ePHI was affected, support the breach-notification obligations to patients and OCR, and document everything. Better, we work to prevent it: the same managed detection and response with a 24/7 SOC, MFA, encryption, and email security that stop most breaches before they become reportable. See emergency IT & ransomware recovery.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

PCI DSS Compliance: at a glance
## What PCI DSS requires, and what it really protects
If your business takes cards, PCI DSS applies. Assuming your POS vendor 'handles it' is exactly how small merchants end up breached and fined. Ghosxt makes PCI compliance practical for Central Coast retailers, restaurants, hotels, and service businesses: the right SAQ, real network segmentation, secure payment systems, and the monitoring to back it up, from an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience who secures payment networks the way they should be.
The businesses that get breached are almost always the ones that assumed someone else had it covered. PCI is not just paperwork. It is the difference between a card-skimming attack that goes nowhere and one that ends up on the local news.

## See what PCI compliance takes for your business
## Segmentation is the whole game
## PCI DSS compliance FAQs
Q: Who needs to be PCI compliant?
A: Any business that accepts, processes, stores, or transmits credit card data, which is nearly every retailer, restaurant, hotel, and service business that takes cards. PCI DSS is not a law, but it is a contractual requirement from the card brands and your payment processor, and non-compliance can mean fines, higher fees, or losing the ability to take cards at all.
Q: What is an SAQ and which one applies to me?
A: A Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) is how most small merchants validate PCI compliance. Which one you use depends on how you take payments: SAQ A for fully outsourced e-commerce, SAQ B for standalone terminals, SAQ C for integrated POS, and so on. Picking the right SAQ is half the battle, and we determine it for you before anything else.
Q: Do I really need network segmentation?
A: It is the highest-leverage thing you can do. Segmentation separates the systems that touch card data from everything else: guest Wi-Fi, back-office PCs, security cameras. As a result, the scope of PCI (and the cost of compliance) shrinks dramatically, and a breach on the guest network cannot reach the payment systems. For most small merchants, segmentation is the whole game.
Q: Do I need quarterly vulnerability scans?
A: If your environment is in scope for external scanning (most integrated and e-commerce setups), yes: quarterly scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor are required, plus internal scanning and prompt remediation. We set up the scanning, interpret the results, and fix what they find, so a scan is a routine pass rather than a fire drill.
Q: Isn't my POS vendor handling PCI for me?
A: Partly, and that is a dangerous assumption to leave unchecked. A modern POS or payment terminal handles part of the burden, but your network, Wi-Fi, access controls, and staff practices are still in scope and still your responsibility. We map exactly where your provider's responsibility ends and yours begins, then close your side.
Q: What if we have a card-data breach?
A: A card breach can trigger forensic investigation, fines, and mandatory notification, expensive and reputation-damaging. We help you respond and, far more importantly, prevent it: segmentation, secure POS, MFA, and monitoring that stop the intrusions that lead to card theft. See cybersecurity and emergency IT.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.
## Take cards with confidence, not crossed fingers

## Cyber insurance compliance FAQs
Q: What controls do cyber insurance carriers actually require?
A: Most carriers now ask about the same core set: MFA on email, remote access, and admin accounts; managed detection and response on every endpoint; backups with an offline or protected copy and a tested restore; a documented patch cadence; email security; security awareness training; a written incident response plan; device encryption; vulnerability scanning; and a current risk assessment. Miss one of the first three and most small businesses see a decline or a repriced premium.
Q: Our renewal questionnaire doubled in length. Can you help us answer it?
A: Yes, and it is the most common way Monterey, Santa Cruz, and San Jose businesses find us. We answer the technical sections accurately, pull the supporting evidence from our consoles, and hand your broker a clean package. For a managed client, a renewal is an hour of review, not a six-week project.
Q: We were declined or repriced. Is that the end of it?
A: Almost never. Carriers usually cite the specific gaps, most often MFA, MDR, or untested backups. Close them, document them, and resubmit. Start about 60 days before your renewal date so there is time to implement and generate evidence; our cyber insurance renewal checklist walks the full timeline.
Q: Do you replace our insurance broker?
A: No. Ghosxt is engineer-led, not a licensed broker: we build the controls and produce the evidence, and your broker handles coverage, policy language, and carrier selection. Everything we do is operational guidance, not insurance advice, and it works best paired with a broker who writes cyber policies for California small businesses.
Q: Can a claim really be denied over a questionnaire answer?
A: Yes. The application is a representation of fact, and many policies carry a failure-to-maintain exclusion: if post-incident forensics contradict a control you attested to, the claim is at risk. That is why we keep controls enforced and evidence current between renewals, not just in the week the questionnaire is due.
Q: What does getting ready actually cost?
A: Less than most owners expect, because the usual gaps are configuration on tools you already own rather than new licenses. Ongoing readiness is built into our managed plans, and our pricing is published, no call required. The free assessment sizes your actual gap before you spend anything.

A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

Ransomware Recovery & Emergency IT Support: at a glance
## If you're in an active incident right now
Do these four things while you call us. One: disconnect affected machines from the network (unplug the ethernet or disable Wi-Fi) but do not power them off, since that can destroy evidence and recovery options. Two: do not pay the ransom or contact the attacker yet; that decision comes after we know what is recoverable. Three: do not delete the ransom note or wipe anything: it helps identify the strain and the right decryptor. Four: call (831) 204-0501 so a senior engineer can start containing the spread.

## Ransomware & emergency IT FAQs
Q: We're down right now: how fast can you respond?
A: Call (831) 204-0501 immediately. We begin remote triage as soon as you reach us and mobilize on-site across the Central Coast for active incidents. Critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment. The faster we can contain it, the more we can save, so do not wait to call.
Q: Should we pay the ransom?
A: Not as a first move, and ideally not at all. Paying funds the next attack, does not guarantee a working decryptor, and often marks you as a soft target for repeat extortion. If you have recoverable backups, which we work to confirm first, that changes the decision. We help you make it with clear eyes, alongside your insurer and counsel.
Q: Can you recover our data without paying?
A: If cloud backup was in place before the attack, mail and files come back from a point in time the attacker could not touch. Whether anything else is recoverable depends on what is intact. Where backups are partial, we rebuild from whatever clean copies exist and tell you plainly what is and is not recoverable. What is intact is exactly what the first hour of triage determines.
Q: We don't have good backups: can you still help?
A: Yes. We contain the incident, preserve evidence, and rebuild from whatever clean copies exist: unaffected endpoints, cloud copies, and vendor tooling where it applies. We are honest about what is and is not recoverable, and we focus on getting you operating again as fast as possible while preserving what evidence matters.
Q: Do you work with our cyber-insurance carrier?
A: Yes. We document the incident, scope, and remediation the way carriers and breach counsel require, coordinate with their incident-response process, and produce the report you need for the claim. If you are unsure whether to notify your carrier first, call us and we will walk you through it.
Q: How do we keep this from happening again?
A: Recovery is step one; hardening is step two. After you are back online we close the door the attacker came through (managed detection and response with 24/7 monitoring, phishing-resistant MFA, cloud backup, and segmentation) so the same incident cannot repeat. See cybersecurity and backup and disaster recovery.

## Break-fix vs. managed IT FAQs
Q: Is managed IT more expensive than break-fix?
A: On the invoice, managed IT is a predictable monthly fee while break-fix looks cheaper until something breaks. Once you count downtime, emergency rates, lost productivity, and the security incidents break-fix does nothing to prevent, managed IT is usually cheaper over a year, and far more predictable. The expensive option is the surprise $8,000 month after a ransomware hit.
Q: We're small. Do we really need managed IT?
A: Small businesses are targeted precisely because they tend to run break-fix with no monitoring and no one watching. You do not need an enterprise contract, but you do need the basics maintained: backups, patching, MFA, managed detection and response. For very small teams we offer a flat-rate Tiny Team plan that delivers exactly that without enterprise overhead.
Q: Can we start with break-fix and switch to managed later?
A: Yes, and many businesses come to us that way, usually after a scare. We can start by stabilizing and documenting your environment, then move you to managed IT once the immediate fires are out. The sooner monitoring and backups are in place, the fewer emergencies you will have.
Q: What's included in managed IT that break-fix isn't?
A: The proactive half: 24/7 monitoring, patching, cloud backup, managed detection and response, a help desk you can call anytime, and someone who actually knows your environment. Break-fix only shows up after something is already broken. It is reactive by design, with no incentive to prevent the next problem.
Q: How is managed IT priced at Ghosxt?
A: Transparently and upfront. We publish our plans (per-user managed tiers plus a flat-rate Tiny Team option) so you can see the cost before you ever talk to us. See pricing for the current plans.
Q: Is it cheaper to hire an in-house IT person or outsource?
A: For most small teams, outsourcing is cheaper. A 10-person team runs $1,250 to $2,500 a month on our published per-user tiers ($125 to $250 per user). A single in-house hire costs more before benefits are even added: California's median annual wage is $79,570 for a computer user support specialist and $106,440 for a network and computer systems administrator, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics program, which works out to $6,631 to $8,870 a month in base wage alone. And one hire only covers the hours they work, with no backup when they are out. See the full math in the cost comparison above.

## Managed IT cost: common questions
Q: Is $150 per user a month normal for IT support?
A: Yes, for fully managed IT. Our own published tiers are $125, $175, and $250 per user per month, so $150 sits between the first two. The better question is what the $150 includes. If managed detection and response, backup, or security awareness training show up as separate line items, compare total monthly cost, not the headline rate.
Q: How much does IT support cost for a 10-person office?
A: On our published pricing, a 10-person office pays $1,250 a month on Core Managed IT ($125 per user), $1,750 on Secure Growth ($175 per user), or $2,500 on Compliance & Continuity ($250 per user), plus $1,500 one-time onboarding on the Microsoft 365 default scope. Add $200 a month for a server and $50 for a firewall if you have them.
Q: What does managed IT cost for a business with 2 or 3 employees?
A: $600 a month, flat, for 1 to 4 users on our Tiny Team plan. That includes monitoring, help desk, patching, managed detection and response, MFA, email security, cloud backup for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, and security awareness training. One-time onboarding is $1,000.
Q: Is managed IT cheaper than hiring an IT person?
A: For most small teams, yes. One in-house hire costs a full California salary plus benefits and still leaves you uncovered when that person is sick or on vacation. The calculator on our pricing page compares the two for your headcount, and for most small teams it comes out roughly 73 to 79 percent less than building the same skills in-house.
Q: Is there a setup fee for managed IT?
A: Yes, a one-time onboarding fee. It's $1,000 for Tiny Team. For the per-user plans it depends on headcount: 5 to 15 users is $1,500, 15 to 30 users is $2,500, 30 to 50 users is $4,000, and above 50 is a custom quote. Those fees cover the Microsoft 365 default scope. Google Workspace and Apple fleet onboarding is scoped and quoted separately.
Q: Do I have to sign a long-term IT contract?
A: Our standard agreement is 12 months, with no price increase during the term. Leaving early during that first term costs 50% of the remaining months. After 12 months you can cancel with 30 days' written notice and no fee. If you want no commitment at all, month-to-month is available from day one at 15% more.
Q: Do you charge more for Google Workspace or Macs?
A: The monthly per-user price is the same. Any laptop or phone enrolled in device management adds $15 per device per month, and Google Workspace and Apple fleet onboarding is scoped and quoted separately instead of using the Microsoft 365 onboarding fee.
Q: Do you serve Salinas, Monterey, and Santa Cruz?
A: Yes. We're based in Salinas and work on-site across Monterey County and in Santa Cruz, San Benito, and Santa Clara counties, and remotely anywhere in the US. The prices on this page are the same in every city.

## FAQs about IT services for trucking companies
Q: Can you support our ELD vendor (Samsara, Geotab, Motive, Omnitracs)?

We routinely integrate with all major ELD platforms for driver-app sign-in, single sign-on, retention of DVIRs and HOS records, and making sure the back-office side (TMS, dispatch, accounting) talks to the ELD vendor's APIs reliably. Q: We have C-TPAT validation coming up. Can you help?
A: Yes. Our C-TPAT compliance services page covers the cybersecurity criteria in detail. For trucking and logistics specifically, we cover the IT documentation, access controls, password policies, and data-protection requirements CBP asks about during validation, and we provide the audit trail that survives a real review.
Q: How do you keep dispatch software up during a network outage?
A: Layered. Most small fleet operators get one ISP and call it a day. We add a second uplink (cellular failover or a second wired ISP), put the dispatch system on equipment that auto-fails over, and make sure your driver and customer-facing portals stay reachable when one path drops. Dispatch is the heart of the operation; it should not run on a single point of failure.
Q: We have drivers across multiple states. Can you support remote endpoints?
A: Yes. Driver laptops and tablets are some of the trickiest endpoints in any environment because they live offline often, connect to shared cellular networks, and get used by different people. We deploy MDM, managed detection and response, forced disk encryption, and conditional access so a lost or stolen device is contained, not catastrophic.
Q: We had a wire-fraud attempt against accounts payable. Can you prevent this?
A: Yes. Wire fraud against trucking AP is one of the most common attacks we see. The pattern is consistent: an attacker compromises an inbox, installs a hidden forwarding rule, watches for an invoice, then sends a lookalike email asking for the wire to go to a new account. We block the pattern at multiple layers: MFA on every mailbox, conditional access rules, automated detection of forwarding rules, banking process changes (out-of-band verification), and ongoing security awareness training for AP staff.

## FAQs about IT services for manufacturers
Q: Can you support legacy CNC controllers still running Windows XP or Windows 7?
A: Yes. Most shops we walk into have at least one machine running an out-of-support Windows version because the controller software does not run on anything newer. We do not pretend the controller can be patched. We isolate it on a dedicated network segment, lock down what it can reach, monitor it for behavior changes, and put the rest of the shop floor behind a firewall so a compromise of one machine does not become a compromise of the whole plant.
Q: We are bidding on a DoD subcontract that requires CMMC 2.0. Can you help?
A: Yes. CMMC 2.0 Level 1 is largely about basic safeguarding of FCI. Level 2 is the heavier lift: 110 controls aligned to NIST SP 800-171, plus an SSP, a POA&M, and either a self-assessment or a C3PAO assessment depending on the contract. We build the documentation, deploy the controls, run the assessment prep, and produce the artifacts a defense prime or the DoD will actually ask for. A federal-grade engineering background makes that work straightforward, not theoretical.
Q: We have engineers across three sites who need to share CAD files. Best way?
A: Depends on file size, version-control needs, and whether export controls are in play. For most small shops, a properly configured PDM system on a single hub with replicated read caches at the satellite sites beats trying to share through generic cloud storage. We have built variants of this for engineering teams running SolidWorks PDM, Autodesk Vault, and lighter setups on shared file servers. The deciding factor is usually whether the data falls under ITAR, EAR, or a customer-specific protection requirement, because that changes the architecture.
Q: We had a ransomware scare on the shop floor. How do we segment OT from IT?
A: Start with a real inventory: every device on the shop floor, what it connects to, what it actually needs to talk to. From there it is a network architecture project: a dedicated OT VLAN, a firewall with explicit allow rules between OT and IT, no broad RDP or SMB across the boundary, and isolated management for the OT side. Most shops we work with did not have an OT VLAN at all when we started. That is the first fix. The second is monitoring, because you cannot defend what you cannot see.
Q: We make medical devices. What does FDA 21 CFR Part 11 mean for our IT?
A: Part 11 is the FDA rule for electronic records and electronic signatures in regulated activities. The IT side is access control, audit trail integrity, system validation documentation, time-synced logs, and a retention policy that survives an FDA inspector asking for a record from four years ago. For small medical device manufacturers we layer those requirements into the ERP, QMS, document control, and email systems, and we keep the validation paper trail current as systems change.

A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## FAQs about IT services for healthcare practices
Q: Are you a HIPAA-compliant IT provider? Do you sign a BAA?
A: Yes. We sign a Business Associate Agreement with every healthcare client before we touch a system that handles PHI, and we operate as a covered Business Associate ourselves. The BAA is the legal floor. The actual work is the controls underneath it: encryption, access management, audit logging, breach response readiness, vendor management, and the documentation a Security Risk Analysis will ask for.
Q: We had a lost laptop. Was it a breach? Do we have to report?
A: It depends on whether the laptop was fully encrypted with a recognized standard at the moment it was lost. If it was, HIPAA treats the data as unreadable and unusable, and no reporting is generally required. If it was not, you are inside the 60-day breach notification clock for individuals (or 60 days from year-end for breaches under 500 people if you choose annual reporting). Either way, we run the forensic checklist, document what was on the device, and produce the artifact you need for OCR if it gets asked for.
Q: Our EHR vendor handles security. Why do we still need an MSP?
A: The EHR vendor handles the security of the EHR application and the data it stores. They do not handle the laptops, the workstations at the front desk, the back-office printer that scans charts, the wifi network the practice runs on, the email system the staff uses, or the backups of anything outside the EHR. That entire surface area is the practice's responsibility, and it is most of the actual HIPAA risk surface. That is where an MSP fits.
Q: We are a small practice (3 providers). Is full HIPAA compliance really required?
A: Yes. HIPAA does not have a small-practice exemption. The Security Rule applies the same way to a three-provider practice as to a hospital, and the OCR fines on small practices have not been theoretical. What does scale with practice size is the level of effort: a three-provider practice does not need a CISO, but it does need a Security Risk Analysis, a written set of policies and procedures, encryption everywhere, MFA everywhere, training, and a documented incident response posture.
Q: We do telehealth. What changes for the IT side?
A: Telehealth widens your environment by every endpoint that connects to it: home laptops, personal phones, vendor platforms, and the network paths between them. The IT side is endpoint hygiene on whatever devices providers use, MFA on the telehealth platform, a BAA with the platform vendor, encrypted recordings (or no recordings if your policy says so), and a documented patient-consent workflow that captures the right disclosures. The HIPAA enforcement discretion that covered casual telehealth tools during the public health emergency is gone; the standard rules apply now.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## FAQs about IT services for hospitality
Q: We use Toast, Square, or Clover. Do you support our POS?
A: Yes. We do not resell the point-of-sale platform, but we run everything around it: the network the terminals sit on, the segmentation that keeps guest Wi-Fi away from payments, the Microsoft 365 tenant and back-office identity, device management, and the backup of the surrounding records. We have hands-on experience with Toast, Square, Clover, Lightspeed, SpotOn, TouchBistro, and Aloha on the restaurant side; Oracle OPERA, Mews, and Cloudbeds on the lodging side; and Commerce7, WineDirect, and Tock for tasting rooms and wine clubs. Keeping your PCI scope small and your terminals online is the job.
Q: Does guest Wi-Fi really have to be separate from our POS and back office?
A: Yes, and it is the most common thing we fix first. Guest Wi-Fi, the payment terminals, the back-office PCs, and the cameras and door locks each belong on their own network segment, not on one flat network behind the modem the internet company dropped off. If a guest's infected phone shares a network with your POS, an attacker who lands on the guest side can reach the side that processes cards. We build separate VLANs with a captive portal for guests, so visitors get internet and nothing else. It is inexpensive, it is an explicit PCI expectation, and it is exactly what a cyber-insurance underwriter looks for.
Q: How do you keep us taking cards when the internet or the power goes out?
A: We plan for it before it happens. That means a cellular or 5G internet failover so card processing keeps clearing when the wired line drops, a UPS on the network and payment gear so nothing crashes hard, a documented offline-payment procedure your managers have actually practiced, and a generator plan for kitchens, walk-ins, and crush equipment where spoilage is on the line. On the Central Coast this matters because the PG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff program can take power for 12 to 72 hours during fire season. A dark dining room or tasting room should not also be a closed one.
Q: We're seasonal with high turnover. Can you handle fast onboarding and offboarding?
A: That is exactly what identity-first IT is for. Every person gets a named account and a named POS login, never a shared server PIN that the whole shift knows. Roles are scoped so a seasonal host or tasting-room pourer can do their job and nothing more, and company tablets and phones are under mobile device management so a lost device can be wiped. When a seasonal hire leaves, we disable one named account and the access is gone the same day, instead of changing a password twenty people memorized. This protects your audit trail, your PCI posture, and your guest data through every summer and harvest surge.
Q: Is a small restaurant or winery really a target for ransomware?
A: Yes. Hospitality is one of the most-attacked industries because downtime turns into lost revenue instantly and a lot of card data flows through it. You do not have to be a big resort. The attacks that took down major hotel and casino operators in recent years started with a convincing phone call to a help desk and a reset password, and that same social-engineering playbook scales down to a busy independent restaurant or a Carmel Valley tasting room. The defenses are the same proven controls everywhere: MFA on every account, managed detection and response on every device, monitored email, a verify-by-phone rule for money and passwords, and a tested backup so a bad night is a restore instead of a ransom.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## Adjacent services for SMB offices

## FAQs about IT services for SMB offices
Q: We almost got hit with a wire-fraud email. Can you prevent this from happening again?
A: Yes. Business Email Compromise is the most common attack we respond to at small offices, and the playbook is consistent. We harden the mailbox layer (MFA everywhere, conditional access, modern auth only), we deploy real-time detection for new inbox forwarding and reply-to rules, we configure DMARC, SPF, and DKIM properly so lookalike domains are easier to block, and we rewrite the AP or trust-account confirmation process so a wire instruction cannot land without an out-of-band phone call to a known number. The combination is what stops repeat attempts.
Q: We use Microsoft 365 and it works "fine." Do we still need help?
A: A default Microsoft 365 tenant is not secure. The security baselines that matter (modern auth only, conditional access, mailbox audit logging, retention, data loss prevention, external sharing controls, app consent governance) are off or wide open by default and the average tenant we walk into has not touched them. The mail works; that is not the same as the tenant being safe. Hardening a tenant is a one-time project that pays for itself the first time it stops an account takeover.
Q: We have 12 people across two offices. How do we share files securely?
A: For most small offices, a properly governed SharePoint and OneDrive footprint beats a network file share or a generic cloud-storage account. The wins are at the governance layer: matter or client folder structures with explicit access lists, retention rules that match your professional standards, audit logging, and a default-deny posture on external sharing. Multi-office connectivity is handled at the identity layer (single sign-on, conditional access by location and device) rather than by routing all traffic through a single corporate VPN.
Q: Our cyber-insurance renewal added 30 questions. Can you help us answer them?
A: Yes. Cyber-insurance underwriting has gotten sharper across every carrier and the questionnaire is now the cheapest way for them to set your rate. We answer the technical sections (MFA coverage, managed detection and response deployment, backup resilience, mean time to patch, incident response plan, vendor risk management, privileged access) with a real number rather than a checkbox, and we close the gaps in advance so the renewal lands at the rate you want.
Q: A partner is leaving and we need to lock them out fast. What does that look like?
A: Same-day offboarding done right is a fifteen-minute procedure if the systems are set up for it. We script the revocations: email and SSO disabled at a specific time, MFA tokens revoked, VPN and conditional-access exceptions removed, mailbox forwarded to a designated partner for client continuity, mailbox put on legal hold for the retention window, and any matter-system access logged for the audit. If you do not have those scripts ready when a partner walks out, the right time to build them is before the next one does.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## FAQs about IT services for property management
Q: We use Yardi, AppFolio, or Buildium. Do you support those platforms?
A: Yes. We do not resell the property management platform, but we run the infrastructure that surrounds it: the workstations and laptops in each leasing office, the Microsoft 365 tenant, the identity layer, the backup and restore policy, and the network plumbing that keeps the office in sync with the cloud-hosted platform. We have hands-on experience with Yardi Voyager and Breeze, AppFolio, Buildium, Entrata, RealPage, Propertyware, and Doorloop. Integration tuning for rent payment processors, tenant portals, screening services, and accounting hand-offs is part of the work.
Q: Our leasing staff use personal phones for tenant photos and texts. Is that a problem?
A: It is a real one. Tenant photos, lease documents, and signed communications on a personal device that is not under any policy is a fair-housing and tenant-data exposure waiting to happen. We deploy app-protection policies through Intune that secure the property management app and the work mailbox on a personal phone without fully enrolling the device. The staff keeps their phone; the company keeps the data; if the staff member leaves, the work data is wiped without touching personal photos.
Q: How do you handle the resident Wi-Fi versus the office network at each property?
A: They are different problems and they need different networks. Resident Wi-Fi is a tenant amenity that needs throughput, captive-portal sign-in, and per-resident isolation so one infected device cannot reach another. The leasing office network needs identity-bound access, conditional access on the property management app, and visibility into who is touching tenant records. We design them as fully separate VLANs (or fully separate ISPs at properties with the budget) with no path between them. The resident side never sees the leasing side.
Q: We had a maintenance vendor get phished and forward an invoice with new bank routing. How do we stop that?
A: This is the most common attack we respond to in property management. The pattern is reliable: a vendor mailbox gets compromised, the attacker quietly watches an invoice cycle, then sends a lookalike message with new wire instructions. We harden the AP layer with MFA on every mailbox, deploy real-time detection for inbox forwarding rules, configure DMARC and SPF properly so spoofed vendor domains are easier to block, and rewrite the AP confirmation process so a vendor routing change cannot land without an out-of-band phone call to a known number at the vendor.
Q: A property manager just gave notice. They had access to twelve buildings. What does cleanup look like?
A: Same-day if the system is set up for it. We script the revocations against the property management platform, Microsoft 365, every vendor portal the manager had access to, the resident-facing tools, and the door-access system if you run smart locks at the properties. Mailbox goes on legal hold for the retention window. The manager is locked out as part of the payroll exit process. Without that scripting, a multi-building cleanup is the kind of two-week project nobody does well, and that is where the data leaks happen.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## FAQs about IT services for engineering and architecture firms
Q: Our SolidWorks or Revit files take five minutes to open over the VPN. What fixes that?
A: Almost always one of three things: the file is being streamed over a saturated VPN, the PDM or vault server is undersized for the working set, or the workstation is rendering on a CPU that does not have enough RAM or GPU. We diagnose by measuring rather than guessing: file-open profiling, vault round-trip times, GPU and memory utilization at the workstation. The fix is usually a PDM read replica at the satellite office, a local cache layer for hot working sets, a workstation refresh to a Pro GPU and 32 GB minimum, or a VDI / cloud workstation pattern if the team is fully remote. Five minutes routinely drops to 15 to 30 seconds.
Q: Can engineers work from home without copying CAD files to a personal device?
A: Yes. The pattern is remote-workstation-first, not file-sync-first. We deploy GPU-passthrough VDI or cloud-workstation platforms (Frame, Workspot, Azure Virtual Desktop, or an on-prem RDS / Citrix setup, depending on file sizes and budget). The engineer signs in from any device, the CAD work happens on a workstation we control, and no file ever lands on the engineer's personal laptop. Conditional access and disk-encryption verification gate every session.
Q: Our project deadline is Friday and the file server is making weird noises. What is your response time?
A: Critical incidents like this carry our 4-hour notification commitment, and you reach the engineer directly. "Weird noises" before a deadline is the moment to call us, not after the server has actually failed. We pull SMART data, check vault health, validate the last backup, and stage a known-good restore target in parallel so that if the box does fail, the cutover is prepared in advance rather than started from scratch. If the noises are actually a fan or a coil whine and the box is fine, we still document the assessment so the next round of disk-failure indicators is not ambiguous.
Q: We are submitting on a federal infrastructure project that mentions NIST 800-171 or CMMC. Does that apply to us?
A: It depends on whether the contract gives you access to Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). Federal civil engineering work for Army Corps, NAVFAC, FAA, or BLM increasingly includes flow-down clauses that require NIST SP 800-171 controls (and CMMC Level 1 or 2 by phased timeline). If you only ever see Federal Contract Information (FCI) without CUI, Level 1 self-assessment is usually enough. If CUI is involved, you are looking at Level 2. We help engineering firms read the actual clauses in the bid package, scope the boundary, and stand up the controls before the contract starts, not after.
Q: How do you back up a 4 TB BIM or PDM vault without saturating our internet for two days?
A: When a firm runs on Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, most project data already lives in SharePoint, OneDrive, or Google Drive, and that is what our cloud backup covers: held outside the tenant, restorable to a point in time, with no full-copy upload competing with your project traffic. A project vault that lives on a server needs its own backup design, and we scope that with you rather than promise a generic answer.
Q: Who will I actually talk to?
A: Ulises Paiz, the owner, directly. There is no tier-1 queue and no offshore call center: the engineer who knows your environment answers the phone, and critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.

## Nonprofit IT on Google Workspace: common questions
Q: How much does IT support cost for a small nonprofit?
A: $600 a month flat for 1 to 4 people, or $125 to $250 per staff member per month for 5 or more. A 9-person team on Secure Growth ($175 per staff member) is $1,575 a month, plus $15 per Mac for device management. Contractors who only need their accounts protected are priced per identity and quoted with your proposal.
Q: Our ops director runs Google Workspace. Do they have to give it up?
A: No. We can take over administration completely or work alongside your ops director as a backstop. Either way, we set up a separate super admin account, enforce 2-step verification, and document who holds admin rights.
Q: Is Google Workspace backed up automatically?
A: Not in the way most people assume. Google keeps deleted items for a limited time and lets an admin restore a deleted account for about 20 days, but that's retention, not backup. Cloud backup for Google Workspace keeps a separate copy of Gmail and Drive that you can restore from after those windows close.
Q: Do contractors and volunteers need a company laptop?
A: No. People on their own laptops are covered per identity: 2-step verification, identity monitoring, access limited to what they need, and the account suspended when their work with you ends. We don't manage their personal devices.
Q: Do you offer a nonprofit discount?
A: Ongoing managed IT is billed at the published rates on our pricing page. What we donate is setup: Ghosxt Cares covers Microsoft 365, domain, email, website, and DNS setup for one Monterey County 501(c)(3) per quarter. The bigger savings usually come from Google for Nonprofits and TechSoup, and we help you use both.
Q: Can you support staff who work from home in different states?
A: Yes. Everything on this page works remotely: Google Workspace administration, identity monitoring, device management, and help desk. Macs ship to staff homes and enroll themselves, and a departing staffer's laptop can be locked or erased from anywhere.

## Remote Mac team IT: common questions
Q: Can my company see what I do on my work Mac?
A: Device management on its own doesn't read your files, email, messages, or browser history, and it doesn't track location. It sees the Mac's model, macOS version, installed apps, and whether security settings are on. Other tools on a managed laptop see more: the monitoring agent reports health and patch status and lets us run maintenance remotely, our remote support tool can see your screen during a support session, the security agent watches for attacker behavior, and DNS filtering sees which sites are looked up so it can block malicious ones. And your employer, as the admin of your work account, can access work email and files.
Q: How do you set up a Mac for a remote employee you've never met?
A: Through Apple Business Manager. You buy the Mac on your business account, it ships sealed to the employee's home, and on first boot it enrolls itself in device management and applies your settings and apps. Nobody in IT has to touch it.
Q: What happens to the laptop when a remote employee quits?
A: Their account is suspended and the Mac is locked or erased remotely in the same offboarding step. Because it's enrolled through Apple Business Manager, we can prevent or clear Activation Lock, so their personal Apple Account can't strand it. Once it's back and erased, it re-enrolls itself for the next hire.
Q: Can you support employees in other countries?
A: Yes. Identity monitoring and 2-step verification work wherever someone signs in, and device management works anywhere the Mac has internet. To be straight about hours: our help desk runs 8am to 6pm Pacific, Monday through Friday, which is evening to early morning for staff in India. Critical incidents carry our 4-hour notification commitment.
Q: How much does managed IT cost for a remote team on Macs?
A: $125 to $250 per person per month, plus $15 per Mac for device management. A 10-person team on Secure Growth ($175 per person) is 10 × $175 + 10 × $15 = $1,900 a month. Teams of 1 to 4 pay $600 flat, plus $15 per Mac. Apple fleet onboarding is scoped and quoted separately.
Q: Do we need Apple Business Manager?
A: For zero-touch setup, yes. It's free, and it needs a free D-U-N-S number for your business. Macs outside Apple Business Manager can still be managed, with more manual steps and less control.

This experience directly benefits Ghosxt clients. The same practices that work for large organizations (proper documentation, security-first design, thorough testing, systematic problem-solving) work just as well for small businesses. They just need to be adapted appropriately.

## What Makes Our Approach Different
### Direct Communication
We explain what's happening with your systems in plain English. If something breaks, we tell you what broke, why it broke, and what we're doing to fix it permanently, not just patch it temporarily. No runaround, no jargon, no excuses.
### Enterprise Architecture for Small Business
The infrastructure practices that work for large organizations (proper Active Directory design, network segmentation, security hardening, systematic monitoring) work just as well for small businesses. You get enterprise-quality infrastructure without paying for a 20-person IT department.
### Proactive, Not Reactive
Custom monitoring systems catch issues before they impact your business. Rather than waiting for systems to break, we identify patterns and fix problems during maintenance windows, not during your busiest workday.
### Complete Documentation
We document everything about your infrastructure. Network topology, configurations, passwords, procedures: all organized and accessible. You're never locked in or left guessing if something happens to us.

## Frequently Asked Questions
Have questions about working with Ghosxt? Here are answers to the most common questions we receive from potential clients.
Q: Do you work with businesses outside California?
A: Yes. While we're based in Salinas and available for on-site work in California, most of our support is delivered remotely. We've structured our services for efficient remote management, which keeps costs down while maintaining responsiveness. We work with clients throughout the United States.
Q: What size businesses do you work with?
A: Any California business that needs reliable IT and cybersecurity but doesn't have (or want to hire) a full internal IT department. Tiny teams of 1–4 fit our Tiny Team Managed Security plan; teams of 5+ use per-user pricing on Core, Secure Growth, or Compliance & Continuity. We've worked with shops as small as 3 and as large as 60+.
Q: Do you require long-term contracts?
A: No. While we recommend at least 3-6 months to properly architect and stabilize your infrastructure, we don't lock clients into multi-year contracts. Good service should earn your continued business, not a contract.
Q: How quickly can you start?
A: For new managed service clients, we typically need 2-4 weeks to properly onboard: audit existing systems, document everything, implement monitoring, and establish baseline operations. For urgent project work, we can often start sooner.
Q: What if we just need help with a specific project?
A: We're happy to discuss project work (network redesign, cloud migration, etc.) separate from ongoing managed services. Some projects lead to managed service relationships, others don't. We're comfortable with both.
Q: How do you handle after-hours emergencies?
A: Critical incidents get a 4-hour notification commitment, with a direct line to the owner. Our monitoring systems watch 24/7 for critical issues. For planned after-hours work (infrastructure upgrades, migrations), we schedule in advance to minimize business disruption.

Title: Ghosxt Cares – Free IT for Monterey County Nonprofits

# Ghosxt Cares
Free IT foundations for Monterey County nonprofits. We donate our time and expertise to help local 501(c)(3) organizations build a modern IT foundation: at no cost for our labor.
100% free labor · For Monterey County 501(c)(3) nonprofits
Ghosxt Cares: at a glance
## Good IT shouldn't be a luxury for nonprofits.
Ghosxt was built by an engineer who spent years securing systems where the stakes were high and the standards were higher. The same care that protects a business shouldn't be out of reach for the organizations doing the hard work in our community.
Too many Monterey County nonprofits run on a personal Gmail, a forgotten domain, and a website nobody can update, not because they don't care, but because real IT help has always cost money they'd rather spend on their mission. Ghosxt Cares is our way of closing that gap: we donate the setup so the technology fades into the background and the work can come first.
## Everything to get your org online: done right.
Ghosxt is a Salinas-based managed IT provider. Through Ghosxt Cares, we set your organization up with the tools it needs from day one.
We walk you through Microsoft's Nonprofit program and configure your tenant, admin accounts, and security defaults.
Professional email on your domain (e.g., you@yourorg.org). We handle DNS records and mail flow configuration.
A clean single-page website deployed on your hosting: enough to establish your online presence.
Domain routing, MX records, SPF/DKIM/DMARC: configured correctly from day one.
A 1-hour walkthrough so your team knows how to use what we built.
A plain-language record of your accounts, domains, and settings, so you own your setup and are never locked in.
## Three simple steps.
No long forms. No commitment. Just a short conversation to see if we're a fit.
### Reach out
Email us or book a quick call and tell us a little about your organization.
### We confirm eligibility
We verify your 501(c)(3) status and Monterey County base, then map out what you need.
### We schedule & build
We set everything up, walk your team through it, and hand over the documentation.
## Your costs, kept minimal.
Our labor is free. You only cover the third-party costs we have no control over.
## Do you qualify?
Ghosxt Cares is limited to keep quality high. Here's what's required.
- Active 501(c)(3) organization based in Monterey County
- Limited to 1 organization per quarter
## Ready to get your org online?
Send us an email and we'll follow up to confirm eligibility and schedule your setup. Spots are limited to one organization per quarter.
Questions first? Email cares@ghosxt.com.
## Questions, answered.
Q: Is it really free?
A: Our labor is 100% donated: you pay nothing for the setup work. The only costs are third-party fees we can't waive, like domain registration (about $12/year) and any hosting. Microsoft 365 is free or deeply discounted for eligible nonprofits.
Q: What's the catch?
A: There's no catch. We're a local managed IT provider giving back to the community that supports us, and there's no obligation to ever become a paying client.
Q: Who qualifies?
A: Active 501(c)(3) organizations based in Monterey County. We take one organization per quarter so each one gets our full attention.
Q: How long does setup take?
A: Most setups are completed within a couple of weeks of our kickoff call, depending on domain registration and Microsoft's nonprofit approval timelines.
Q: Do you support us after setup?
A: Setup includes a one-hour onboarding session and handover documentation so your team is self-sufficient. If you ever want ongoing managed support, it's available separately, but it's never required.
Q: We're a nonprofit outside Monterey County. Can you help?
A: Ghosxt Cares is focused on Monterey County for now, but reach out anyway. Depending on your needs we may be able to help remotely or point you to the right resource.

## What we do
### Managed IT Services
Fixed-fee, all-inclusive day-to-day IT for small business teams of all sizes, from flat-rate Tiny Team Managed Security for 1 to 4 users up through per-user tiers for larger teams. Monitoring, helpdesk, patching, identity, backup, and quarterly strategy. The relationship most small businesses should have with their IT provider, run by one senior engineer instead of a ticket queue.
### IT Help Desk & Support
Live, US-based IT help desk and end-user support: direct access to the owner, remote and on-site fixes, and a real engineer who knows your environment instead of a tier-1 script. Password resets to printers to Microsoft 365, handled remotely. Included with managed IT.
### IT Consulting & vCIO
Strategic IT leadership without a full-time CIO salary: an IT roadmap, technology budget, security and compliance strategy, risk assessment, and vendor-neutral advice. Available standalone or included as quarterly planning on every managed plan.
### Cybersecurity
Government-grade cybersecurity controls, sized and priced for small business. Managed detection and response (MDR), identity hardening, MFA, cloud backup for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, vulnerability management, security awareness training, and incident response. Built around the discipline of an engineer with DoD infrastructure experience.
### Cloud Services & Microsoft 365
Microsoft 365 done right, Azure where it earns its place, hybrid where it makes sense. Tenant hardening, Conditional Access, M365 migrations, and SharePoint architecture without the buzzwords or the lock-in.
### Backup & Disaster Recovery
Cloud backup for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace covering mail, files, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Drive, a written business continuity and disaster recovery policy, and an annual independent risk assessment. The kind of backup program a DoD engineer would trust their own data on.
### Network Design
Properly designed networks. VLAN segmentation, real firewalls, enterprise wireless, multi-site VPN or SD-WAN, full documentation. No more flat networks defended by an ISP router with a default password.
### Web Development
Custom websites and e-commerce that load fast, rank well, and actually convert visitors into customers. Built from scratch by the engineer who will keep them running, hosted on infrastructure we control end-to-end.
### C-TPAT Compliance
C-TPAT cybersecurity for importers, carriers, freight forwarders, and 3PLs. CBP-aligned controls and documentation that hold up under validation, without disrupting your operations.
### Co-Managed IT
Already have an IT person or team? We augment them (help-desk overflow, after-hours help on request, and cybersecurity and compliance depth) filling the gaps without replacing anyone. Enterprise tooling and a senior engineer behind your in-house IT.
